title: The NO-IRI Trial: Can Inhaled Nitric Oxide Help Protect the Liver During Transplantation?
official: The NO-IRI Trial: Inhaled Nitric Oxide for the Prevention of Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury in Liver Transplantation
summary:
Liver transplantation remains the only cure for patients with end-stage liver disease. Despite continuous advances in medical care, ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) (tissue damage that occurs when blood supply is restored to an area that has been deprived of oxygen) remains a major contributor to complications with the newly transplanted liver. A key factor involved in the development of IRI is reduced nitric oxide (NO) availability in the body. NO is a transmitter the sends signals to protect cells against injury and to maintain healthy blood vessels. The investigators have designed a randomized clinical trial (RCT) investigating the use of inhaled NO to reduce IRI in liver transplantation.

A total of 110 patients receiving a deceased donor liver transplant will be randomly assigned to receive either inhaled nitric oxide or a nitrogen gas placebo during surgery and for up to 24 hours afterward. The investgators will then collect postoperative data from medical records to evaluate indicators of liver cell injury, liver function, and other common post-transplant complications. The investigators anticipate that participants who receive iNO will have reduced IRI injury and better transplant outcomes than those who received the placebo gas.

Participants will be followed for one year after transplantation. The findings will help determine whether inhaled nitric oxide can improve liver transplant outcomes and support its use as part of routine transplant care.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

1. Adults aged 18 years or older at time of enrollment.
2. Receiving a deceased donor liver transplant.

Exclusion Criteria:

-1. Patients undergoing multi-visceral transplantation. 2. Patients receiving a living donor transplant. 3. Patients undergoing liver retransplantation. 4. Patients with a diagnosis of hepatopulmonary syndrome. 5. Patients with severe baseline methemoglobinemia. 6. Patients with a G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) deficiency. 7. Patients in acute liver failure. 8. Patients with left ventricular dysfunction resulting in low ejection fraction.

9\. Patients with portopulmonary hypertension.
